utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. My name is Miodrag Stojanovic, and together with my colleagues, I represent General Ratko Mladic. I'd like to go through some of your documents, and I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing I wanted to ask you is this: Do you recall having given a statement to the Prosecutor's office here at the Tribunal on the 10th of April, 2008 with regards to these events?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, could we provide a clean hard copy of the statement to the witness, and I'd kindly ask that it be with him throughout the testimony because I will have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are in open session now. I will put some questions to you, and I would kindly ask you not to refer to your position at the time in any way. I'm interested in this: As of the 4th of April, 1992, you were in the area of Sarajevo as a member of the then-JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: It is not. I was in the area of Sarajevo between -- as early as the 2nd of December, 1991 when I was relocated there with my unit and the command of the 5th Military District from Zagreb to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And as of the 4th of April, 1992, you were deployed at the forward command post at Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, that is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You worked in the same body that you stayed with during your work in the 1st Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes. I was with the same military organ in Zagreb and anywhere else throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of June, 1992, you were transferred to the 1st Krajina Corps and were moved to Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in and around Sarajevo, were you ever in a position to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I met General Mladic in Crna Rijeka. I believe it was on the 12th of May, 1992. We were there together until the 3rd of June, when I was transferred to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you mind sharing your experience and your view with the Court about General Mladic at the time and his position. What kind of officer was he?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: It is not fully appropriate for a junior officer to address a senior officer, but now that you ask the question before this Tribunal, I can tell you this: In Crna Rijeka, I was only there for a few days with General Mladic, and I wasn't in his immediate environment though and I did not receive tasks from him because I was General Tolimir's subordinate. What I could observe, though, in the course of those few days was that he was way too busy. Every morning at 7.00 a.m., he flew by helicopter from Crna Rijeka to close to Sarajevo to negotiate the release of cadets from Sarajevo. That was his main preoccupation while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of June, 1992, you assumed your duties at Manjaca, pursuant to an order of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps. Is the date correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, around the 15th. That is when I assumed my duties at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: RM051

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at paragraph 18 in your statement where you say that the Manjaca camp was well organised. What did you mean by that? What did you mean when you said that the Manjaca camp was well organised?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Well, my claim may be subjective, admittedly. However, if one could assess the regularity of all the camps in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Manjaca would occupy a very high first place. Some people don't like that, or cannot understand that, because of the reports in the media. However, what I saw, what I knew, and what we did at Manjaca, I would say that Manjaca was one of the best regulated camps in Bosnia. I could corroborate that by the way people were received in the camp, by the attitude towards the detainees, the frequent visits of international organisations, the daily visits of journalists, the International Red Cross. There was a nutritionist who paid visits to the camp every day from 9.00 to 5.00 in the afternoon. These are the claims that I stand by. What I said then I still adhere by, and I will always maintain the same position. I had the good fortune to witness that my efforts were adopted by Commander Popovic and my subordinates, and we tried our best to be as humane towards those people, because we truly believed that those -- all those people had to leave the camp on their two feet, healthy and alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we pay attention to paragraph 19, as well as to paragraph 20 in your statement. And let's provide some clarification about the attitude of the civilian police who brought detainees to Manjaca and the relationship between the civilian police and yourselves who had a duty to take the prisoners over. Let's take things one at a time. From what moment did you, as a professional, believe that a detainee started to become a custodian of the Manjaca camp command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question, as interpreted, was: "From what moment did you, as a professional, believe that a detainee started to become a custodian of the Manjaca camp command." I don't understand the question. That's how you were interpreted. I don't understand how a detainee becomes a custodian of a camp.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: From which moment did the camp become the custodian of any particular detainee?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question is the result of paragraph 20 in the witness's statement. It says: "We would not consider these prisoners as our own prisoners until they went through the admission procedure and until the moment they were entered into the ledgers." This is the sentence authored by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was this: You were a professional. What did you base your conclusion on? And what did you imply by that sentence? Could you provide some sort of an explanation for the benefit of the Trial Chamber? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: We adopted a normal logic, according to which a detainee became a detainee at Manjaca once he was officially admitted. We had a commission that admitted prisoners into Manjaca. That commission comprised two military police officers, a doctor who was also a detainee, and one of my men. After a complete checkup and after the registration in medical books and in the ledgers, groups of ten detainees would be taken into their future accommodation. And from that moment on, they would be considered as detainees at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before that moment, before they were registered and physically taken over, in whose custody were those future detainees, in terms of their physical security and the safety of their person and their property?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: As you may have seen, Manjaca camp is on a mountain. It's quite isolated, and people were mostly brought over by trucks or buses. MUP members were in charge of bringing them in, if they were transferred from other collection centres. In principle, those were MUP members until the moment when they handed them over to us. Those people were in the custody of MUP members, i.e., of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be more about that in the documents that I intend to show you. You have already spoken about something that I wish to ask you next. If it occurred that one of the future detainees came into harm's way during the transport and if you learnt about that, I'm asking you this: As a soldier, what would have been your duty? What were you supposed to do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: We admitted only living people into the camp. If one of them died during the transport, obviously we did not admit such people. We did not have a service that would be in charge of burials. We would return those dead people to be transported, and we -- we had them transported back, and they were escorted by the same people who had brought them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Through your regular activities in the form of daily reports, you recorded such personal knowledge about this possible commission of crimes. You did report that to your superiors. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: By all means, that would be the most important thing that would happen on that day, and, of course, I'd include that in my daily report and make my superior aware of that, and he probably reported up the chain of command, all the way to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that, according to regulations from 1992, dealing with members of the police or paramilitaries was within the civilian judiciary, not the military judiciary, in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That's right. We've clarified that several times here before this Court. That's the way it was. If a member of the MUP would be outside the army, then his misdeeds would be dealt with by a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You personally, in view of the position that you held - and we're not going to mention it - had no way of knowing of whether information about such misdeeds committed during transportation were provided to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska through reports. You don't have any knowledge about that. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I don't have any such information. However, it would be logical, and I think that my department and my immediate superior did that, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we agree that, according to the system of subordination, the superior of your superior, whose name you mentioned here, was Mr. Stevilovic, the security organ in the 1st Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I immediately moved onto this other person because Stevilovic was killed on the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then this would be the right moment to ask you about this. You said that he was killed on the 5th of July. Would it be correct to say that he was killed in the territory that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, in the depth of the territory of the Republika Srpska? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He was killed on the 5th of July, 1992, near Kotor Varos. He was ambushed there by a roadblock by the HVO, and Stevilovic was killed on that occasion. Also Markovic and another soldier who was in the vehicle. Practically, they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Manjaca camp, as you've testified in relation to these events, all the way up to its disbandment, two detainees, Filipovic and Bender, saw their tragic deaths; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And, in a way, I was astounded by that, surprised by it, saddened by it, because I thought that that kind of thing could not happen in view of the organisation that we had there. It did happen. It was explained in a way within half an hour. The perpetrators were identified. An on-site investigation was carried out by the MUP authorities and the court authorities. The pathologist did his job. And it was a bit late, but, nevertheless, the perpetrators were prosecuted, and they were sentenced to very serious time in prison; 14 years, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's the next question I'm going to put to you. We're also going to use a document. However, now that you've opened the subject, you do know that before the court in Banja Luka these persons were prosecuted, and they were convicted. We are talking about several persons; right?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That's right. It is four men, and three of them were sentenced to long-term prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the scope of your own authority, when you found out about this crime, you did everything that was your duty on the basis of the rules of service, based on the Geneva Conventions, and you informed all the relevant authorities about this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Everything was done. We did whatever this kind of thing merits. That is to say, an on-site investigation team arrived, a pathologist arrived. The bodies were handed over. We thought that the case had been resolved, as far as we were concerned, and then other services dealt with the funeral arrangements and the prosecution and everything else. However, we, at Manjaca, did whatever we could at that very first moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask that we look at document 65 ter 08779. 08779. While it is being brought up in e-court, Your Honours, may I say that this is a daily report. I would just like to ask -- very well. It is a daily report of the 26th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the direct examination, there were questions as to whether criminal proceedings were instituted against the persons who were in the Manjaca centre. I would like to ask you to focus on paragraph 4 of this report in which it says, inter alia: "All prisoners have been processed in the Bosanska Dubica public security station and criminal reports have been submitted to the basic public prosecutor's office in Bosanska Dubica. They were brought to the Manjaca camp only for accommodation and guarding purposes." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Could you please tell the Court what this means, from a procedural point of view, that criminal reports were filed against certain persons?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: When a criminal report is filed against someone, that means, from a procedural point of view, that this criminal report provides all the evidence, for and against, in terms of this person having committed a certain crime, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there is a pre-criminal proceeding that takes place before a criminal report is filed? A suspect interview is conducted, evidence is collected, and all of this is provided along with the criminal report, stating that there are reasonable grounds to believe that a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I fully agree with your statement. Let me just add something. The Prosecutor asked me whether I knew of any case when these persons who were in Manjaca were prosecuted before a court of law, and my answer was, I don't know. However, these are pre-criminal or pre-trial proceedings. So your question is quite different in relation to that, and my answer is that I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be the essence of my question. So the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force in that year, in 1992, stated that we had an investigative judge and investigative proceedings, and then pre-criminal/pre-trial proceedings would involve operative work, collecting evidence, and the basic suspicion that would be contained in the report. And then it is up to the investigative judge and the prosecutor to file for an investigation to take place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Since I was studying criminalistics and criminology at the time, that is exactly how things were, as you stated them. So I fully agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I seek some clarification. Earlier, you were asked about any criminal proceedings. It even included any type of action taken against any of these people who were suspected of criminal action. I did understand that question and your answers to be in relation to those who you investigated, either on the basis of the material that was provided to you, but where you took an active part in the investigation of crimes committed by the detainees. Was that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood Madam Prosecutor's question to pertain to all the people who were in Manjaca. I understood the question to be whether I know whether anybody had been prosecuted for what they did before they came to Manjaca. However -- and my answer was that there were no court proceedings that I had been aware of. Court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I do understand that the document that we're looking at at this moment is about persons for which your role was limited to keep them in detention, and that others had investigated potential crimes and others were responsible for reporting and taking action. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. In this document, it says that criminal reports were filed against these persons by the MUP organs from Bosanska Dubica and that there's nothing for us to do there. Or, rather, that they were there in order to be kept there, and to be there until they're called by a court of law or someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we had two categories of prisoners: Those who you investigated, where you were responsible for investigating any suspicions against them, and others for which you just provided accommodation, not being involved in any way in the investigations conducted against them. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. You understood it as I meant it. That was my experience, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Yes, Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated a little earlier, sir, at page 35, lines 18 to 23, that these people who came to Manjaca and about whom your answer to the Prosecutor was that you were not aware of any court proceedings, is that people who had been investigated before they came to you. My question to you is: Of those that were investigated by you, were there any court proceedings instituted as a result of any or all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We filed criminal reports for about ten people from Manjaca. These were active-duty military officers of the JNA who had deserted and joined the enemy force. They were taken prisoner, and they were brought there. And then we filed criminal reports with the military court in Banja Luka. On several occasions, we also took them to this military investigative prison. However, an indictment was never issued. There was no judgement ultimately, so they were brought back to Manjaca. Let me just explain this a bit. This is exactly the way it was. This was in the case of some ten persons who were former JNA officers who had deserted from the JNA, who joined the enemy force, who were taken prisoner, and then they were brought to Manjaca, and then we filed these criminal reports against them. And several times they were taken to this military investigative prison in Banja Luka, but they were returned. And I don't know -- actually, to be more specific, I don't know whether an indictment was issued. However, I know that there was no judgement that was passed, and I know that they went to third countries, together with all the other detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. With regard to those who were prisoners of war - in other words, who came from what you may have regarded as enemy army, not those who deserted - were there any that were charged or against whom court proceedings were instituted as a result of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you so much. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have one more question regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that at that time, in June 1992, whether, as a matter of fact, Bosanska Dubica did or did not have a prison the size which could accommodate such numbers of people?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I don't know that. But if I try to reason logically, and based on overall information, I suppose they did not have a prison of that size.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me conclude this topic with this question: While working there, save for the ten you mentioned, were there -- did you send any other criminal reports to the competent judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: In relation to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Save for about a dozen reports for the active military personnel, I did not submit any other criminal reports. I submitted Official Notes, though, and the statements taken from the people we interviewed. That material was then sent for further assessment and potential processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 65 ter 03057. Your Honour, while waiting for it, I wanted to say that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Since the previous translation continued, Madam Registrar, you told us, may I take it, that this document was admitted as P218.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which document, Madam Registrar? I'm sorry. Is it 08779?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 030507, that was called now and is on our screens, is admitted as P218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And should not be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps I may continue now with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, Witness, please have a look. It reads that 29 people from the villages of Velagici and Pudin Han were processed in Kljuc municipality. "Light was shed on the role of certain persons in the organisation and the launching of an attack on the police patrol held check-point as well as on the military column in the Busije location." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It continues: "The circle is widening and our processing is adjusting accordingly." My question is this: What kind of information did you obtain in your operative work concerning the events in Velagici and Pudin Han that are referred to in this daily report?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: It was about an attack on a military column at Busije. It was returning from Knin. I think they were mostly young soldiers. The event took place before I arrived from Crna Rijeka. It was still being cleared by way of interviews with people at Manjaca. During the attack on the military column, five soldiers were killed. It was most probably done by the people from the villages of Velagici and Pudin Han near Kljuc. They set up an ambush at Busije, and when the column arrived, they opened fire at the vehicles, killing five soldiers. I don't know many details about it since I wasn't there at the time, but things were being slowly cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it also refer to the part of paragraph 1 where there is a mention of light being shed on the role of certain persons in the organisation and the launching of an attack on a check-point manned by a police patrol?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to paragraph 4 of the report, then, which reads: "On order of Colonel Anicic, prisoners Ahmet Hodzic and Ismet Focak from Sanski Most, who had been of considerable help to the military organs during the confiscation of weapons, have been released." The first question: Please tell the Court who is Colonel Anicic?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, but Colonel Anicic was either commander or the assistant commander for morale of the Sanska Brigade. He intervened asking that the two men be released from Manjaca. Irrespective of the fact they were brought there, they had significantly assisted the soldiers and military organs in Sanski Most. Thus, he believed that they should be released, and it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this an exception or are you familiar with more examples of that nature?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was an exception, but it didn't happen often. There were a few cases of similar nature while the camp at Manjaca existed. Some officers intervened, asking that this or that person be released as they had been captured or imprisoned by mistake. Perhaps people from the police asked for it or something of the kind. There weren't many such cases. Perhaps another two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Concerning the system of control over the camp or centre, since it seems we have a semantic problem, up to whom was it to determine who would be released in such cases, from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That's a good question for my sake, too, because I was neither outside nor above the system of command. This document is phrased in such a way that one may conclude it was up to me to decide. This intervention by Anicic and the release of the two people went through the regular command channel. I believe the assistant commander for morale, Colonel Vukelic, requested that personally. He was from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. He ordered, in a way, to see whether we had any additional information on the people and to release them. And this wasn't done by me. I told you I was not part of the command system or the decision-making system. The camp commander put it all in writing and made a decision to have them released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I seek clarification about the word "release". When you say people were released, and earlier we looked at a document - perhaps you remember - you said some people were considered to be extremists by those who brought them to Manjaca but you thought could be released. Now, if we're talking about "release," were then people released and free to go home again, or were they led to another place and not free to choose their own destination, when, as you said it, released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case of those people who were released from the camp and then went onto third countries, they were simply released as part of the procedure. They were released and it could be interpreted in a different way, as if they only went outside the parameter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I'd like to know is whether they were told, What do you want? To go home or to go to a third country? What do you want to do? Or were they just released, to be transferred to a third country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The International Committee of the Red Cross interviewed everyone, and they had their statements about whether they wanted to leave, and where, which third countries. As regards -- that -- that is regarding the group departure via Karlovac. In the case of these two -- perhaps I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The large number of people, as you said, that were released, were they ever given an opportunity just to return home, to their own homes, where they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the group departure of the 700 people? Is that what you're asking me about? The International Committee of the Red Cross took them to third countries. Their first station, though, was in Karlovac, and there they could decide whether they would go on to another country or return home, but we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give them an opportunity to go home? We have seen in your report that you said that many of them were no combatants, had no arms, were not in uniform. Apparently in this report you state clearly that there's no reasonable suspicion of them being criminals or having committed crimes. Did you offer them to go home before they were put in the hands of the Red Cross to be brought wherever? Did you say, You're innocent. What do you want? Do you want to go home? Then please, if I could say so, take the next bus home. Of course, there were no buses. I am aware of that. But did you offer them to go wherever they wanted to go before the Red Cross took care of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It mostly happened with the cases of people who were selected and were younger than 18 or older than 65. But, still, we didn't release them just like that. It was a state of war. You cannot just leave them around Manjaca in an isolated area. There was a procedure in place to hand them over. We usually handed them over to the Merhamet, the Muslim humanitarian organisation, and they took them away, the people we had released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say that happened with the ones below the age of 18 and the elderly but not for the rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the sick. Some 90 of them were pardoned and sent to Geneva for treatment. So the young, the old, and the sick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the able-bodied men who had not been combatants, who had not worn a uniform, who had no arms, were not given an opportunity to just return to their homes through whatever procedure but were given in the hands of the Red Cross. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. By the way, Mr. Stojanovic, you earlier indicated - and I thought I'd wait for a second - when you talked about the persons which were responsible for the death of Filipovic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Bender. You said: "We're also going to use a document." Is that still to come? Because I've not -- or is one of the documents you've used, until now, related to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We are yet to come to that document. It's one of the daily reports, and I will advise you of the particular document, as I will have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I will be patient. But I think we first should take a break. If the curtains are down, the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom, and we take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Stojanovic, could you, meanwhile, tell us how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In keeping with what I had announced, I believe I will take two and a half hours in total. Thus, I believe I can conclude before the end of hearing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I address the accused briefly. We are now re-starting with a delay of eight to nine minutes. The Chamber was informed that this is due to you visiting the toilet, Mr. Mladic. You are advised to go to the toilet at the beginning of the break. We scheduled the breaks early at the request of the Defence -- the short breaks at the request of the Defence. If the same would happen again, and if you have not used the opportunity to go to the toilet at the beginning of the break, then the Chamber will just start and proceed. Although we have considered whether or not to deduce the time now from time from cross-examination, we have decided not to do that yet. This is what I wanted to convey to you. We'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Just a moment. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the curtains be pulled up again. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to call up P215. This is another daily report issued on the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at the last paragraph together. In it, it says that a certain number of detainees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Stojanovic. The document is admitted under seal. You should have --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I don't think that my questions arising from that document would comprise the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the document should not have been broadcasted if it is under seal, and you should have mentioned it when calling the document. I'm not saying that you should go into private session but that you should have given notice of that fact when calling the document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, it says a certain number of detainees would like to volunteer to go to the front line to prove their mettle. "It is still difficult to ascertain the exact number but this could be ascertained on the spot and if called up by the organ for morale." What is this about? Could you tell the Trial Chamber? Was this idea ever implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Our operative intelligence were bored in the camp. According to our operative intelligence, the detainees were bored in the camp. That's why we wanted to go to the front line to escape the enclosed space. We didn't know what their number was, and I can't see it in the document. This was forwarded to the organ for moral guidance. This never came to fruition. Nobody was ever sent to the front line from the camp. This was just an initiative of sorts which never came to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your impression? Was it really the will of those people or was it forced upon them?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I really don't know what to say. I don't have a position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at P219. It's another document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek one clarification. What were they supposed to do at the battle-fields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this would be my interpretation of the document and of what I can remember: Those people were loyal to the Serb forces. There were ten Serbs up there in Manjaca camp. Five of them volunteered to go to the battle-field, and I suppose that this can be interpreted as some Muslims also wanting to go to the battle-field, as any other combatant. That's how I interpret things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then to fight the Muslim forces? Is that your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know who the warring parties were in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Muslims against the Serbs, the Muslims against the Serbs and Croats, Croats against the Serbs, and Muslims against the Muslims. So everybody fought everybody else. They would be part of our forces. And then whether they would have been used against the Muslims or the Croats, I really can't tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document. This is a daily report which was issued on the 5th of July, 1992. In paragraph 1, it says: "... a group of 268 prisoners of war" --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I believe it's P227.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P215. And I have the right document on the screen, both in B/C/S as well as in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document 219, Mr. Stojanovic, not 215. 215, you are now done with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. P219. I apologise. P219. The document on the screen is P219. I apologise, and I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The previous one, it could have been unclear on the record. To that extent, I -- although it is listed as under seal, it does not appear on the record, although I may have said that it was under seal. This one certainly was under seal. Now, Ms. Hochhauser, in your description of the document of 219, P219, you say it's dated the 5th of June. This document, however, bears a different date. Is that your mistake or is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, that is my mistake in the description because I can see that the ERN numbers match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, it should be 5th of July. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, sir, in the first paragraph, you say that a group of prisoners from Sanski Most has been completely processed. Official records have been made. The statements have been taken, which is sufficient paperwork to submit criminal reports against the individuals who merit to have criminal reports against them issued, which shall be done by the authorised officials from the SJB Sanski Most. My question: Within the system that you were part of at the time, who was the one who was supposed to look at your Official Notes and issue a criminal report and send it to the authorised prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: If you are referring specifically to this paragraph here, it is absolutely clear that criminal reports would be submitted by the individuals from the SJB Sanski Most. And if you're asking me in general terms, as to who issued criminal reports against people at Manjaca, if we conducted interviews and if we took statements and collected evidence, then it would be us who would have done that. So what is your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question should be worded in the following way to be more clear: It arises from this report, if my understanding of it is proper, that criminal reports will be submitted, drafted and submitted, by the authorised officials from the Sanski Most SJB; right?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then in the following paragraph that I would like to draw your attention to, you say, while mentioning persons between the ages of 60 and 80 [as interpreted], that they should possibly be returned to their original places of residence? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the idea of the author of this report? Where were these people supposed to return to when they left the Manjaca centre?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: They should have been taken over by the Sanski Most SJB if they were from Sanski Most, which I see that they were. So they would be taken over by the officials and returned to their homes, people aged over 60 and people under 18. Those people are not subject to military obligation, if there is no evidence that they had committed a crime, for example, if they had -- had not killed a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that those people who had undergone triage and it was established that they did not commit any crimes, were they allowed, or would they have been allowed to choose their place of residence in the future? Would they have been allowed to return to their original place of residence?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes. Those persons did not merit to be treated as prisoners of war, according to our assessments and according to the information available to us. That's why we suggested that the Sanski Most MUP should have come to pick them up and return them to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at P227. Again, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to pay attention to paragraph 2 in this document. The date on the document is 8 July 1992. In this document, it is stated that during transport from Sanski Most to Manjaca, 24 prisoners died and that the probable cause was lack of oxygen; that such conduct was extremely inhumane and unprofessional; and that the people who died were not admitted and they would not be considered as ever having been prisoners of war. Is this the confirmation of your previous words when you spoke about those whom you considered as prisoners of war admitted to the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, quite. This is very clearly spelled out in this document, and that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In all that, when we're talking about the army and trying to defend the army, before you admitted such a person whom somebody had brought over from Sanski Most, Kljuc, Prijedor, or Kotor Varos, did you have any idea as to whether such a person met with the Geneva Conventions standards when it comes to him being treated or being considered as a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I must say that when they first presented themselves, we admitted them through the work of our commission in all the cases. If that person came with a note or a document, that note or that document would be studied in order to create a picture about the person. If there are no such documents, we interviewed our future detainees, and it depended on the skill of the interviewee how much they would be able to get from -- from the interview, how much they would be able to get from the interviewee. But, in my view, it was not important what crime they committed. If they were brought over to the camp, if they were alive and well, they would be admitted. Nobody was turned out -- turned down. Nobody was refused admission. Everybody was admitted. Then we interviewed them, we processed them later, and then we would see how things transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I ask one clarifying question. If I look at the description of, as it is said, "the large majority of prisoners having no weapons, nor having actively participated in the organisation or the implementation of the armed rebellion," doesn't that just simply make them civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? People would say that they did not carry arms, that they did not participate in fighting, that they were taken from their fields, but that did not necessarily have to be the case. It was very difficult for me up there, if we're talking about me or anybody else from the camp, it was very difficult for us to guess whether people were involved or not. It was a camp where people were guarded, pending a decision of a higher command or the president himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not what the documents says. The document does not say it is characteristic that they told us that they had no weapons. No. The document says it is characteristic, as was the case with previously processed prisoners. So that it is similar to those already processed, that a large majority of prisoners brought to the Manjaca camp had no weapons, nor have they actively participated in the organisation or implementation of the armed rebellion. This fact makes it difficult to collect and compile documentation on criminal acts necessary for functioning of illegal activities. I read this as they are not combatants. They are not involved in any crimes. That makes it difficult to have any documentation on illegal activities. Now, if you say, Well, it was uncertain. It still could be. What do you need to make someone a prisoner of war, for him to be a combatant? Or would you say even if they are civilians, if it has not sufficiently been established, we will nevertheless treat them as prisoners of war, although our information tells us that they had not actively participated in the armed rebellion, they had no weapons, and they were not wearing any uniforms. Is that sufficient to make someone a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my report, and that was the impression I had. It doesn't have to be correct. But my report was sent to someone else to decide on these matters. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not see any suggestion here to immediately release these persons because there's no reason to consider them prisoners of war. I do not see any such suggestion in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe not in this one, but in some reports you will come across such a situation, especially for younger persons and persons over the age of 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed that. Do you have any report in which you suggest that able-bodied men, not being sick, between the age of 18 and 60, should be immediately released and returned to their homes? Because they were not involved in armed rebellion; they were not having any arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are no such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I asked you previously, now I'm going to put the question to you in this other form: When you admit a person at a given point in time, in the centre Manjaca, you do not know and you have no way of knowing whether he meets the standards of prisoners of war, according to Geneva Conventions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Only after you check his initial statement through your own intelligence, when you collect other evidence, it's only then that you can conclude whether what he is saying is correct or is not correct. That is the job of any investigator. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now please take a look at this, paragraph 4 of this statement, where it says that: "The presidents of the municipal and district courts in Banja Luka arrived, as well as prosecutors and the military legal officer of the 1st Krajina Corps. They inspected the conditions in which the prisoners are accommodated and discussed the issue of possible judicial proceedings for the acts they have committed." This is my question: Did the people from the judiciary give you any instructions in terms of how these persons should be dealt with, those who are suspected of having committed serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I don't remember that there were such instructions, such documents, coming from these organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just ask you a very specific question here. Who was it that brought these people from the direction of Sanski Most, when 24 detainees fell victim during the transportation? Do you know these people? Not personally, but do you know which structures they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I don't know them personally, but it was members of the MUP, of the civilian police. They brought prisoners from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask for document P220. I would like to note that this document is under seal as well. It is a daily report dated the 9th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness before you deal with the next document, Mr. Stojanovic. Witness, you were asked by Mr. Stojanovic about the procedure to find out if a detainee was an active combatant before his detention. Mr. Stojanovic put to you, and I quote, page 55, line 4: "Only after you check his initial statement through your own intelligence, when you collect other evidence, it's only then that you can conclude whether what he is saying is correct or is not correct." How did you manage to do that with 23 detainees who were admitted into the camp per day? You told us approximately 23 such initial investigations you had to carry out. How was it possible to gain this additional information in that short period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that we managed to interview 20 to 30 persons per day. It's not that 20 to 30 persons were brought into the camp per day. So we managed to interview that many people per day, my service did. So if there were two or three or four of us, that is how many people we could deal with per day. Again, that meant that we could not actually talk to all the prisoners who were in the camp. What you are asking, how I could do this in such a short period of time, that is a consequence - how should I put this? - of having people brought in who had already been processed. You already heard that some people had been processed in Dubica, Sanski Most, Velagici and other places where they had been taken prisoner. So they were detained there. They were dealt with there. Interviewed, interrogated, statements were taken. So I didn't really have anything to do in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand. Did you have these files from other places you just mentioned at your disposal when interviewing/interrogating these detainees after their arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was one of the problems that I pointed out in many of my reports. Perhaps 10 or 20 of them. I pointed that out, that people were brought in. And it says that they had been dealt with and that there's no documentation. So we would have to ask for it subsequently and then these people from the public security stations would ultimately send these documents in some cases; in others, they didn't. How do I put this? It was done in a very sloppy way, if I can put it that way. This is a problem that we had to deal with up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please let us look at the document in front of you. Could you please focus on paragraph 3, and it says there, in this daily report of the 9th of July, 1992: "Tomorrow, we will receive a visit from the representative of the Muslim humanity association Merhamet, who we are going to hand over our select prisoners, those older than 60 years of age and younger than 18, as well as those who are seriously sick." My question is: How often did Merhamet come to Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: The humanitarian association Merhamet from Banja Luka, headed by Mr. Medic, came once or twice a week. But, as a rule, it was once a week. He would bring humanitarian aid with him. It would be food and clothing. Various supplies for washing as well. This was approved by the corps command. We did not decide on this at all. It was the command of the corps that decided on the basis of his request, and then they would grant it. And then we would know exactly when he would be coming and then he'd ask to see certain persons, or he would give this to the command, asking that this be distributed to everyone. This happened during the first stage of the existence of the camp, that is to say, June and July. After that, the International Committee of the Red Cross started coming, and then Merhamet stopped coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any restrictions in terms of the distribution of humanitarian aid and such-like?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I've already explained that. They would agree with the corps command, and then they would come and distribute this aid. Perhaps they did have some problems of their own, but I did not observe any. People freely distributed this aid that had been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that you are going to hand over to them select prisoners. I'm going to ask you now whether that is what the situation actually was; and were these select prisoners, indeed, handed over to Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Our assessment was that the most expedient thing to do was to hand over to Merhamet those who were younger than 18 and older than 60. Since it was quite a problem in view of the distance to Banja Luka, we'd hand them over to them, and then they would take them to their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again ask you about the categories. I do see that it's the intention to select those older than 60 and those younger than 18 and allow them to return home through the intervention of Merhamet. But earlier in this report, it states that new prisoners are being brought in massively and in large quantities that no selection has been made. "They are bringing in those who shouldn't be treated as prisoners of war because they have been picked up from their homes and off their fields," and then you add that there are also those above 60 and younger than 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted). Nevertheless, they were further detained in this prisoners-of-war camp. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your understanding is correct. That's the way it was. That is what I wrote and that's the way it was. That is the truth. Perhaps -- I tried to point this out, and perhaps I exaggerated a bit so that the people that I was reporting to would really act on this. It's very close to the truth anyway. What you said, that when they were brought again, there were people who were younger than 18 and over the age of 60. That is because Manjaca was like a river, as it were. People were being brought in non-stop in groups and exchanged, and they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there again. I focussed my question exclusively on the people not belonging to these categories of the youngest ones or the elderly, but you treat them as separate categories as well. Those who should not be treated as prisoners of war, because having been picked up from their homes and their fields, and those older than 60 and younger than 18. So a large quantity are just not prisoners of war and, nevertheless, you detained them in the camp of prisoners of war. That is, then, I do understand, correctly understood and I am ignoring at this moment the elderly and the younger ones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you are saying. This category that merits the status of prisoners of war, in terms of their age, but in my estimate they should not be prisoners of war because they were collected from their fields and homes, et cetera. I said that for many of them I did not have any documentation because it hadn't arrived yet. So I tried to speed things up through my own superior, so this organ would send that documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you are not complaining here about lacking documentation. You are saying, "They are bringing in those who have been picked up from their homes and off their fields." So apparently you are aware of that having happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment. It's written there, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the moment when you admit these people who are brought in from Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kljuc, and, as you say, you don't know what their status is, and once they've spent a certain amount of time there at the Manjaca centre, and once you've received certain information and accompanying documentation, and when you assess that a particular person should not enjoy the status of a prisoner of war, according to the Geneva Conventions, what do you do then? What measures do you take? Do help us with this.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I can only share with you what it is that we were doing. Now, as to what should be done, that would entail a much longer answer. So, we did not release any such people from there because we sent our reports to our superior command and awaited their orders. We were part of the command system and did not act on our own initiative. We simply carried out orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that all of them at some point in time, irrespective of whether you believed they should be accorded the status of prisoners of war, as organised by the ICRC, and provided that they signed a statement given freely, that they were allowed to leave Manjaca as it, indeed, happened in February 1992. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That is correct. With the assistance of the ICRC, it was, indeed, done. Several groups left in November and December, and afterwards the camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So all of them were allowed to leave the centre at Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: All of them, yes. So, 4.403 prisoners left the camp and went onto third countries, depending on their country of choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask, just for a moment. When did that happen? When was the camp disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first group of prisoners left on the 14th of November, 1992; the second group, on the 14th of December, 1992; the third group, on the 16th of December, 1992; and the last group, on the 18th of December, 1992, whereupon the camp was closed, when its key was symbolically handed over to this -- I don't know the name anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see that document, Your Honour, and we will rely on it in some future examination. Let us look at P229 next. I'd like to remind you that this document, too, is under seal. Let us have a look at it together, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph, which refers to a visit of the ICRC from Geneva to the centre at Manjaca. Inter alia, it reads that the head of the team thanked for the visit that was enabled to them and the access to every individual prisoner without the presence of any witnesses. I'd like to ask you about your recollection. Were ICRC representatives allowed to enter any part of the camp at Manjaca? Was it possible for them to do so?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Members of the ICRC, as approved by the authorities in Pale and by the Main Staff of the VRS, were allowed to visit the camp and enter any facility, as well as to talk to any inmate. They have been doing -- they did that as of their first visit and during each subsequent visit. Their nutritionist was also present daily in the camp between 9.00 and 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How frequently did the ICRC visit?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I believe I said they came by once a week. And their forces brought in food, mostly fruit, vegetables, and bread, from Zagreb. And that, too, was a type of visit. So it was more frequent. In other words, food was brought in from Zagreb directly to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to page 2 of this report, the second part of the third paragraph, where you say that, in conversation with a number of prisoners, ICRC representatives learned of four people for whom there are reasonable grounds to believe that they were liquidated. Can you recall this? And who were the people in question? What was the status of the four people in question?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Those people had been treated before, either by the military court or another institution. They were supposed to have been in the military investigation prison in Banja Luka but they did not have any room and so they were transferred to our camp. They were not considered POWs; they were simply accommodated there. The camp commander decided to put them aside so that they wouldn't be registered together with the other prisoners. Through their own sources, members of the ICRC found out that information and they wanted to see them, and, indeed, they were shown to them. It's not in dispute in any way. They were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, it says that there was a proposal that the four sentenced men, as it says here and we have their names here, should be transferred to a jail in Banja Luka. Is that a question that was put to you by the ICRC as well?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That is what it says, and that's how it was. We intervened that they be transferred to a facility where they rightfully should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question relating to paragraph 4. There is mention that ICRC representatives stated that the nutrition was poor, as well as hygiene, and Colonel Vukelic reacted to any such statements which were unfounded, as well as Colonel Popovic. Following that, the speaker of the ICRC team calmed down, and they were promised that conditions will be improved, as well as the treatment of prisoners. Can you tell us what kind of conversation was this, and why did it provoke Vukelic and Popovic into reacting?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't say anything other than what is stated here, because I wasn't present at the meeting. I was away, although I no longer remember why. However, once I returned, I was informed about it and that there were some unfounded accusations, as well as that they were discussed. I also heard that the ICRC representatives did correct some of their position but a report to that effect never -- was never sent, which would serve to corroborate that in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this is an opportunity for you to tell the Chamber how food was organised for such large numbers of people, the provision of food.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: The Manjaca camp, as an organisational unit of the 1st Krajina Corps, was supplied by the corps. In other words, the logistics of the 1st Krajina Corps supplied the camp, too. 1992 was a war year. The corridor was cut off, and there were many other issues. The Manjaca camp simply shared the same fate suffered by the rest of the population and the fighters of the corps. In other words, there was a shortage of everything. Much as the fighters at the front lines were short of supply, in terms of specific food types, the inmates at the camp were in the same situation. The number of people increased, whereas the amount of food decreased. That is why we approved that Merhamet should help and we also asked for the assistance of the ICRC, et cetera. Once all of that was set in motion, things were fine. That was the main problem, and it was an objective problem. We all felt it. I didn't eat any better food than the prisoners. I ate what they ate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to clarify something about the corridor. During that period, practically the entire region of Banja Luka was surrounded and cut off from the rest of Yugoslavia, due to intensive fighting in the rear and the inability to provide supplies to the entire area of Banja Luka. Is this statement of mine correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was at that time that the 12 babies died due to lack of oxygen, which couldn't get through from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Some reference is made to the hygienic needs, or needs of hygiene, for the prisoners. How was that organised in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: The possibilities were very narrow. What we could provide as the army were the ABH supplies, which would enable people to wash up at least once a week in field conditions under a tent. We could warm up water for them. They had field toilets. And the conditions in general were adjusted to the overall situation and the number of people. I must say that hygiene was modest or at a low level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. If this would be a suitable time. And I expect you to conclude your examination-in-chief -- cross-examination during the next session. But also would there be any time left for the Prosecution to put some further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your point, Your Honour. I'll reorganise my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. Curtains down first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at 18 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom once the curtains are down. Meanwhile, I'll use the time and address especially the Defence. Last week, Mr. Ivetic was unaware of the practice of providing transcripts of videos to the interpreters before playing such videos in court. The Registry has circulated the Trial Management Meeting paper which sets out the ground rules for these proceedings. However, irrespective of this, CLSS has informed the Chamber that it has always been standard CLSS practice that, in relation to videos, that the parties provide both transcription of the original and its translation as the speed and sound quality makes it impossible to provide simultaneous interpretation of intercepts and videos, and the parties are invited to follow that practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Curtains can be up again. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed. I would like to inform the parties that the Defence still has to respond to the procedure suggested in relation to the next witness to appear, and I would reserve the last ten minutes for that purpose today. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let me conclude this topic before moving on to the next document. I wanted to ask you about your knowledge concerning health care for prisoners in the Manjaca centre?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: As regards the health care of prisoners in the POW camp in Manjaca, the primary health care was provided on the premises. We had two medical doctors at our disposal who were prisoners themselves. We also had our medical technician, a paramedic from the medical centre in Banja Luka, who was there round the clock. The first medical checkup took place at intake, and their health status was recorded in the medical log-book for each person individually. Each prisoner had their status recorded as to whether there were injuries, et cetera. Further medical care was provided in the camp, and we relied on the assistance of the then-medical centre in Banja Luka, the clinical centre in Banja Luka, and further afield, if necessary. That was the short description of the health care provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at P222, which is also under seal. It is a daily report of the 29th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the deaths of Filipovic and Bender, the two prisoners, are referred to here. I hope can you find that. My first question is this: Following the death of these two people, the appropriate judicial and investigative bodies were informed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked that before, I think, or at least the witness testified about it. And it is also in the transcript already, so please move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The report states that possible perpetrators of the crime were identified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That is correct. They were identified within the first half an hour, one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a question regarding that in paragraph 4, around the middle of the paragraph, which reads -- there's a remark that the military police patrol worked independently of their own volition and that no such conduct was ordered, nor did they ask anyone. Today, having all the information, the knowledge you do, and particularly because you told us that the -- these people were tried and sentenced and received high sentences, do you believe this was an independent act of theirs which had nothing to do with any military orders?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: It was utter willfulness, which came about as a surprise to us all up there. We dealt with it, and we asked that they be removed immediately from the camp, that they be relieved of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that done? Were they, indeed, removed from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: On that same day, they were suspended. They were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence in paragraph 4, it says: "We tried to find out whether their murder was commissioned and who did that." What you did mean by that? Was any information obtained through operative work? Did you find out that somebody had ordered their killings?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: When it comes to Omer Filipovic, there was information that he had participated in organising and carrying out certain combat activities in his settlement. And his neighbours, Serbs, who were either members of the military police or the civilian police, and they provided security for the camp, were suspected to harbour hatred against Filipovic. That's why we thought that somebody had told one of those Serbs at Manjaca, You are up there. If you can, kill that person. We also considered that possibility. We investigated that possibility as well, but after our investigation, we did not come to such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the mortal remains of those two prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Filipovic's body and Bender's body as well, there were post mortems were carried out, and their bodies were handed over to the persons in charge at the cemetery, for burial. I don't know whether their bodies were exhumed or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at 07052. This is a 65 ter document. I believe this is another document under seal. This is a report dated 14 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is one of the daily reports which refers to the procedure aimed at disbanding the Manjaca centre, after which all the detainees left the Manjaca camp. What I would like to ask you can be found in paragraph 1, where it says: "After the efficient work on the lineup and after each individual signed a statement as to whether they wanted to be taken away by the International Committee of the Red Cross, around 9.00, we started putting them on the buses." My question is about the statements. What kind of statements were those? Were they written statements? I'll take things one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, it seems that the translation is incomplete, if only because the date is not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14th of December, 1992. Could you send it for review, Mr. Stojanovic, so that we have a complete and reliable translation. Or the Prosecution, if the Prosecution has presented it with this translation. I see Ms. Stewart is nodding yes. So could the Prosecution have the translation reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And could we zoom in to the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look at line 5 in the text, where it says: "Following the successful roll-call, and after each individual signed a statement as to whether they wished to go with the ICRC, the boarding of the buses started at around 0900 hours." Tell the Trial Chamber about the statements. What kind of statements were those, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Those were written statements that all the prisoners of war were supposed to sign if they agreed to be transferred to third countries. And the wording of the statement was, I accept to voluntarily go to a third country in the organisation of the ICRC. I am quoting from memory. I'm paraphrasing. And each of them had to sign that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I would like to ask a clarifying question. You said: "Each of the prisoners of war," but earlier I think we dealt extensively with the question of whether they were prisoners of war. And, as you said, many of them should not be treated as prisoners of war. At the same time, you also told us that from that category, able-bodied men between 18 and 60, that it was never suggested that they would be released, apart from this mass release. So if you say, "Every prisoner of war," do you mean every detainee, or do you really want to say that they all were rightly treated as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to clarify, I can say that everybody who was at Manjaca signed that statement and left to a third country. I don't know what other distinction to make between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was whether you were talking about all people detained, or whether you considered them all rightly to be treated as prisoners of war, despite the various documents we looked through earlier, that many of them were not involved in armed rebellion, did not take up arms, et cetera, and were just sent to Manjaca irrespective of whether they really could be rightly treated as prisoners of war. Would those persons still be detained and be part of this number of detainees being given to the ICRC, or had anything happened meanwhile which made a clear distinction between prisoners of war and those which were unjustifiably treated as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all left with the ICRC. The ICRC was the body that had drafted that statement. They were all treated in the same manner when it came to their release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have preferred if you would have answered my question, but since you apparently do not intend to do so, Mr. Stojanovic, you're invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
