utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, if I could just interrupt for one moment. At page 70 of the transcript, line 11, it records Mr. Stojanovic as drawing up document 5702. I don't think that that correctly captures the 65 ter number of the document that's currently being addressed, so perhaps he could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The document that I called up was 65 ter 07052, and that document is, indeed, on the screen before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he has clarified the matter. Please proceed for another knew minutes, because, as I said, I would like to reserve the last ten minutes for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions about this document, sir. Bearing in mind the entire process, when it comes to the Army of Republika Srpska, was it possible for each of the individuals to perhaps choose not to go to a third country but to stay in the region of Banja Luka? From the point of view of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, they could opt for that. They could stay home, if they were from Banja Luka or from Sanski Most. But, by and large, almost 100 per cent of them chose to go to a third country. They were transported to Karlovac, and from Karlovac, they were then transported to third countries. From Karlovac, they returned home. From Karlovac, some of them rejoined their units. Some of them rejoined either the Muslim army or the Croatian army, and they were recaptured. We had several cases of recapture, when the same individuals were, again, taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me finish with the following question: Before war broke out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while the JNA still existed in 1991, what body was the camp in Manjaca connected to, in terms of establishment lines?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: The Manjaca camp was an organisational unit of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, i.e., it was connected to the army, i.e., to the 1st Krajina Corps, and that line of command went up to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1991, when the JNA still existed and when the 1st Krajina Corps had still not been established, who was the Manjaca camp attached to? Which body?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: If you're asking me about what Manjaca was, what the facilities at Manjaca served, Manjaca was an agricultural farm, i.e., the military institution called Karadjordjevic used to use those facilities. Maybe I did not understand you well the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it part of the then-2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: That was part of the 2nd Military District. Originally, it was part of the 1st Military District and then the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, up to the point when the JNA unit had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was either on 19th or 20th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me finish my cross-examination. You hail from the region, as far as I can understand. I'm being very cautious when I put this question to you. Do you agree with me that that place, that centre Manjaca, had been a working agricultural farm and that it had previously been used as a prison for the prisoners of war captured during the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RM051
utterances.text: Manjaca was a military agricultural farm. It was a cattle farm, where horses and cows were bred, as well as wheat and potatoes, barley. It was a working military agricultural farm. When the war started in 1991, those facilities were used for the accommodation of imprisoned Ustashas who fled before the Serbian forces. In Croatia they closed the bridge in Hrvatska Kostajnica. There were some 370 of them when they were captured. They were brought up there for processing, and from then on, that area or those facilities started being used for prisoners of war. That use started in September 1991. When those prisoners were interviewed, it was disbanded as a camp and then it -- it started being reused in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in December 1992, it was again disbanded as a prisoner of war camp; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I said I would reserve ten minutes for the Defence. You've taken some of that. We apparently are unable to conclude your testimony today, Witness RM051. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. It will not take very long, I take it. And I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is the testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. You may follow the usher, but only after the curtains are down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, meanwhile, I'd like to ask you whether you're ready to make the submissions on the suggested procedure for document charts for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the curtains be drawn up again, and ... Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you first, are we talking about this documents for review chart we have to discuss today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber was not involved in any discussion yesterday. But I think the Prosecution announced that it would start preparing the next witness and use a chart on which he would give his comments, and that you had an opportunity to comment on the suggested proceedings. So not the content of it but the proceedings, as suggested by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see the document from here, and it is, in fact, a document that we are scheduled to discuss today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then since the Prosecution emphasised that it is a unique situation, so we understand that it is only for this witness, and we don't have objection to continue with this witness with this chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand, then, Mr. Groome that this is the only witness with which you would like to follow this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the only witness so far. Now, it may be in the future that we'd have a similarly situated witness that we might seek the same relief, but I certainly wouldn't proceed without requesting to do so, bringing it to the attention of the Defence and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I see that one of my colleagues has, apparently, a copy in his hand. I have not seen it yet. We will look at it. The parties, apparently, do not disagree on this procedure to be used with the next witness. And in the future, we will see. But it will not be standard procedure, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not advocating, at this stage, for that, Your Honour. I would note, Your Honour, that the witness is upstairs now finalizing and reviewing that, so can we proceed on the basis that I will distribute that once it's finalised, and it will be decided, prior to the witness giving evidence, on how to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Chamber would have major objections in relation to this witness because it's limited to that now, we'll let you know as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, if there's nothing else, Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us how much more time you would need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be expecting answers to just two more questions, Your Honours. So it will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as matters stand now, Ms. Hochhauser?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would anticipate about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 25th of September, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.14 p.m.,
